{{short description|Notion for convergence of metric spaces}}
In [[mathematics]], '''Gromov–Hausdorff convergence''', named after [[Mikhail Gromov (mathematician)|Mikhail Gromov]] and [[Felix Hausdorff]], is a notion for convergence of [[metric space]]s which is a generalization of [[Hausdorff distance]].

==Gromov–Hausdorff distance==
[[File:Gromov-Hausdorff distance.png|thumb|How far and how near are some figures under the Gromov–Hausdorff distance.]]
The Gromov–Hausdorff distance was introduced by David Edwards in 1975,<ref>David A. Edwards, "The Structure of Superspace", in "Studies in Topology", Academic Press, 1975, [http://alpha.math.uga.edu/~davide/The_Structure_of_Superspace.pdf pdf] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304082616/http://alpha.math.uga.edu/~davide/The_Structure_of_Superspace.pdf |date=2016-03-04 }}</ref><ref>{{cite arXiv | eprint=1612.00728 | last1=Tuzhilin | first1=Alexey A. | title=Who Invented the Gromov-Hausdorff Distance? | year=2016 | class=math.MG }}</ref> and it was later rediscovered and generalized by [[Mikhail Gromov (mathematician)|Mikhail Gromov]] in 1981.<ref>M. Gromov. "Structures métriques pour les variétés riemanniennes", edited by Lafontaine and [[Pierre Pansu]], 1981.</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Gromov |first1=Michael |title=Groups of polynomial growth and expanding maps (with an appendix by Jacques Tits) |journal=Publications Mathématiques de l'IHÉS |date=1981 |volume=53 |pages=53–78 |doi=10.1007/BF02698687 |url=http://www.numdam.org/item/?id=PMIHES_1981__53__53_0 |mr=623534 |zbl=0474.20018|s2cid=121512559 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> This distance measures how far two [[compact space|compact]] metric spaces are from being [[isometry|isometric]]. If ''X'' and ''Y'' are two compact metric spaces, then ''d<sub>GH</sub>'' (''X'', ''Y'') is defined to be the [[infimum]] of all numbers ''d''<sub>''H''</sub>(''f''(''X''), ''g''(''Y'')) for all (compact) metric spaces ''M'' and all isometric embeddings ''f''&nbsp;:&nbsp;''X''&nbsp;→&nbsp;''M'' and ''g''&nbsp;:&nbsp;''Y''&nbsp;→&nbsp;''M''. Here ''d''<sub>''H''</sub> denotes [[Hausdorff distance]] between subsets in ''M'' and the ''isometric embedding'' is understood in the global sense, i.e. it must preserve all distances, not only infinitesimally small ones; for example no compact [[Riemannian manifold]] admits such an embedding into [[Euclidean space]] of the same dimension.

The Gromov–Hausdorff distance turns the set of all isometry classes of compact metric spaces into a metric space, called Gromov–Hausdorff space, and it therefore defines a notion of convergence for [[sequence]]s of compact metric spaces, called Gromov–Hausdorff convergence. A metric space to which such a sequence converges is called the Gromov–Hausdorff limit of the sequence.

==Some properties of Gromov–Hausdorff space==

The Gromov–Hausdorff space is [[path-connected]], [[Complete metric space|complete]], and [[separable (topology)|separable]].<ref>[[Dmitri Burago|D. Burago]], [[Yuri Burago|Yu. Burago]], [[Sergei Ivanov (mathematician)|S. Ivanov]], ''A Course in Metric Geometry'', AMS GSM 33, 2001.</ref>  It is also [[Glossary of Riemannian and metric geometry|geodesic]], i.e., any two of its points are the endpoints of a minimizing [[geodesic]].<ref>{{cite journal | arxiv=1504.03830 | doi=10.1134/S0001434616110298 | title=The Gromov–Hausdorff metric on the space of compact metric spaces is strictly intrinsic | year=2016 | last1=Ivanov | first1=A. O. | last2=Nikolaeva | first2=N. K. | last3=Tuzhilin | first3=A. A. | journal=Mathematical Notes | volume=100 | issue=5–6 | pages=883–885 | s2cid=39754495 }}</ref><ref>For explicit construction of the geodesics, see {{cite arXiv|eprint=1603.02385|last1=Chowdhury |first1=Samir |last2=Mémoli |first2=Facundo |title=Explicit Geodesics in Gromov-Hausdorff Space |year=2016 |class=math.MG }}</ref>  In the global sense, the Gromov–Hausdorff space is totally heterogeneous, i.e., its isometry group is trivial,<ref>{{cite arXiv | eprint=1806.02100 | last1=Ivanov | first1=Alexander | last2=Tuzhilin | first2=Alexey | title=Isometry Group of Gromov--Hausdorff Space | year=2018 | class=math.MG }}</ref> but locally there are many nontrivial isometries.<ref>{{cite arXiv | eprint=1611.04484 | last1=Ivanov | first1=Alexander O. | last2=Tuzhilin | first2=Alexey A. | title=Local Structure of Gromov-Hausdorff Space near Finite Metric Spaces in General Position | year=2016 | class=math.MG }}</ref>

==Pointed Gromov–Hausdorff convergence==

The pointed Gromov–Hausdorff convergence is an analog of Gromov–Hausdorff convergence appropriate for non-compact spaces.  A pointed metric space is a pair (''X'',''p'') consisting of a metric space ''X'' and point ''p'' in ''X''.  A sequence (''X<sub>n</sub>, p<sub>n</sub>'') of pointed metric spaces converges to a pointed metric space (''Y'',&nbsp;''p'') if, for each ''R''&nbsp;>&nbsp;0, the sequence of closed ''R''-balls around ''p<sub>n</sub>'' in ''X<sub>n</sub>'' converges to the closed ''R''-ball around ''p'' in ''Y'' in the usual Gromov–Hausdorff sense.<ref>{{cite book | doi=10.1007/978-3-0348-9210-0_1 | chapter=The tangent space in sub-Riemannian geometry | title=Sub-Riemannian Geometry | year=1996 | last1=Bellaïche | first1=André |editor1=André Bellaïche |editor2=Jean-Jacques Risler | isbn=978-3-0348-9946-8 |location=Basel |publisher=Birkhauser |series=Progress in Mathematics |volume=44 |pages=1–78 [56]}}</ref>

==Applications==

The notion of Gromov–Hausdorff convergence was used by Gromov to prove that
any [[discrete group]] with [[Growth rate (group theory)|polynomial growth]] is virtually nilpotent (i.e. it contains a [[nilpotent group|nilpotent subgroup]] of finite [[Index of a subgroup|index]]). See [[Gromov's theorem on groups of polynomial growth]]. (Also see D. Edwards for an earlier work.)
The key ingredient in the proof was the observation that for the
[[Cayley graph]] of a group with polynomial growth a sequence of rescalings converges in the pointed Gromov–Hausdorff sense.

Another simple and very useful result in [[Riemannian geometry]] is [[Gromov's compactness theorem (geometry)|Gromov's compactness theorem]], which states that
the set of Riemannian manifolds with [[Ricci curvature]]&nbsp;≥&nbsp;''c'' and [[diameter]]&nbsp;≤&nbsp;''D'' is [[relatively compact]] in the Gromov–Hausdorff metric.   The limit spaces are metric spaces.  Additional properties on the length spaces have been proven by [[Jeff Cheeger|Cheeger]] and [[Tobias Colding|Colding]].<ref name="ChCo">{{cite journal | doi=10.4310/jdg/1214459974 | title=On the structure of spaces with Ricci curvature bounded below. I | year=1997 | last1=Cheeger | first1=Jeff | last2=Colding | first2=Tobias H. | journal=Journal of Differential Geometry | volume=46 | issue=3 | doi-access=free }}</ref>

The Gromov–Hausdorff distance metric has been applied in the field of computer graphics and computational geometry to find correspondences between different shapes.<ref>{{cite book | doi=10.1145/1057432.1057436 | chapter=Comparing point clouds | title=Proceedings of the 2004 Eurographics/ACM SIGGRAPH symposium on Geometry processing - SGP '04 | year=2004 | last1=Mémoli | first1=Facundo | last2=Sapiro | first2=Guillermo | page=32 | isbn=3905673134 | s2cid=207156533 }}</ref> It also has been applied in the problem of [[motion planning]] in robotics.<ref>{{cite arXiv |last1=Sukkar |first1=Fouad |last2=Wakulicz |first2=Jennifer |last3=Lee |first3=Ki Myung Brian |last4=Fitch |first4=Robert |date=2022-09-11 |title=Motion planning in task space with Gromov-Hausdorff approximations |class=cs.RO |eprint=2209.04800 |language=en }}</ref>

The Gromov–Hausdorff distance has been used by [[Christina Sormani|Sormani]] to prove the stability of the Friedmann model in Cosmology. This model of cosmology is not stable with respect to smooth variations of the metric.<ref name="cosmos">{{cite journal | doi=10.1007/s00039-004-0477-4 | title=Friedmann cosmology and almost isotropy | year=2004 | last1=Sormani | first1=Christina | journal=Geometric and Functional Analysis | volume=14 | issue=4 | s2cid=53312009 | arxiv=math/0302244 }}</ref>

In a special case, the concept of Gromov–Hausdorff limits is closely related to [[Large deviations theory|large-deviations theory]].<ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1007/s00209-006-0951-9 | title=Large deviation and the tangent cone at infinity of a crystal lattice | year=2006 | last1=Kotani | first1=Motoko | last2=Sunada | first2=Toshikazu | journal=Mathematische Zeitschrift | volume=254 | issue=4 | pages=837–870 | s2cid=122531716 }}</ref>
